D’Iqaluit à Montréal, « je suis là, quoi: From Iqaluit to Montréal, “I’m here, no matter what.” Meeting Mary Kelly
«Avec la façon dont je suis bâtie, je po: “With the way I’m built, I could hurt people, but I was born to heal them,” says Mary Kelly, who works in the community sector.
« Avec la façon dont je suis bâtie, je p: “With the way I’m built, I could hurt people, but really I was born to heal them,” Mary Kelly says right off the bat. She has worked in community organizing for more than twenty years. This Inuk woman in her forties is outspoken and strong-willed, and she carries herself with a great deal of confidence, which may be intimidating to some but is comforting to many others.
« Je m’étonne que mon énergie légendaire: “I’m surprised my legendary energy didn’t burn out your camera,” she says with a laugh.
Aujourd'hui, elle travaille à titre d'in: Today, she works as an outreach worker in Milton-Parc, where many homeless Inuit live. I sat down with her to write her profile. We met at the offices of Comm-Un, a community organization that offers services and activities to the homeless community of the Milton-Parc neighbourhood.
L’intervenante salue avec enthousiasme t: The outreach worker warmly greets everyone who comes in, sometimes inviting them to sit with her during our interview. Her hair is pulled back in two pigtails, and she is dressed in warm tights and a sweater, ready for her patrol in the cold of the night.
L’atmosphère à Comm-Un est conviviale, o: The atmosphere at Comm-Un is friendly; we can hear other outreach workers and visitors to the centre chatting in another room. It is sometimes noisy, with people going in and out of the offices, passing through the kitchen near us, greeting us and introducing themselves, but it all speaks to the vitality of Mary’s community.
Questionnée au sujet des liens qui l’uni: Asked about the ties that bind her to the Inuit community in Milton-Parc, Mary answers: “Family. Why do you think I get along with everybody?” she asks. “Because you’re connected to them?” I reply. “Because I’m related to them,” she corrects. “I come from the biggest families in the North, on my mother’s side and on my father’s side. I’m related to every one of them. I respect them. I sit down and I listen. I drink and I panhandle with them. I’m no different. I don’t judge them. I’m here for them, no matter what.”
Mary Kelly n'a pas reçu le soutien de sa: Mary Kelly did not get her family’s support growing up in Iqaluit, nor when she moved to the city to attend elementary school. “When I was a kid, I had nobody. There was no mentor guiding me. I had to fund myself. I had to figure everything out on my own. I started at 16 to go to high school, to go to university and college,” she recalls.
« J'ai obtenu mon diplôme d’études secon: “I graduated from high school with distinction. I went to university to design video games. And then what happened was, I was… you know The Matrix? You write code in it. I was dreaming in that damn code. It’s a true story. I still have friends in the field who tell me, ‘I can’t get out of the code, man,’” says the woman in her forties, laughing.
Elle finit par s'inscrire à l'École de t: She eventually enrolled in McGill University’s School of Social Work to take the Indigenous social work program. To say the least, she has a rich and varied résumé: a certified first responder and firefighter, she has worked in sexual health and helped build up the ecosystem of Montréal community organizations serving marginalized Indigenous populations, such as Projects Autochtones du Québec (PAQ) and the Centre d'amitié autochtone.
Elle aborde son travail avec un certain: She approaches her work with a certain sense of humour. “When I was 28, I was a sexual health coordinator. I invited 24 participants from all over Canada to come together in Kuujjuaq. They came from Cambridge Bay, Gjoa Haven, all sorts of different places. In Kuujjuaq, I showed up at the airport dressed as a giant yellow condom, and I told them, ‘Thanks for coming!’” the outreach worker says, laughing.
Alors que ses tâches s’intensifient, Mar: As her responsibilities intensified, Mary Kelly became a mother, which led her to take a break.
« J'ai eu des enfants qui ont 13, 11, 8: “I have kids who are 13, 11, 8 and 6, and the oldest will soon be 22. I was responsible for their lives. Now they’re amazing. They’re so beautiful. They make me so proud,” she says in a soft voice, smiling.
Elle est d’avis que la maternité l'a « a: She believes motherhood “softened” her. “I always thought I was perfect, that I was so good. Until I started to feel bad. When you have kids, you start to feel certain things,” the outreach worker confides. “I couldn’t handle my work. I couldn’t bring it home. I couldn’t do this job,” she explains.
« Lorsque le père et moi avons conclu un: “When the father and I came to an agreement and he took custody of the kids, I was able to go and keep going. And that’s why I’m here, because they’re not with me. I don’t bring anything home, no emotional weight.”
Aujourd’hui, Mary Kelly consacre son éne: Today, Mary Kelly devotes her energy to fiercely protecting her community. She brings her fluency in Inuktitut and her wide-ranging training to the streets.
Shlee, une autre intervenante autochtone: Shlee, another Indigenous outreach worker, comes to sit beside her for a moment. She tells how, one night, Mary Kelly came to the aid of an Inuk man in distress who couldn’t make himself heard on the street.
« J'ai déjà essayé d'intervenir auprès d: “I had tried to step in with this Inuit person before, but he’s not my tribe, not my nation. And yet it was so simple. Mary showed up speaking the language, he listened to her, and he got what he needed,” Shlee explains.
Mary poursuit son récit, sa colère est m: Mary continues the story, her anger evident as she recalls paramedics who pushed her aside. “What’s shitty is that those guys were saying, ‘We don’t want to listen to you.’ I said, ‘I don’t care if you don’t want to listen to me! You’re going to do it because he’s my family. You’re going to listen to him,’” the outreach worker says.
L’homme disait en inuktitut qu'il voulai: The man was saying in Inuktitut that he wanted to go to the hospital, but the paramedics thought he wanted to go to a shelter. Faced with the outreach worker’s insistence, they eventually took the man to the hospital so he could receive medical care. “Imagine this happening to you: you don’t speak the language and they take you somewhere you’re going to die!” says Mary Kelly.
Peu après le départ de Shlee, CJ, une fe: Shortly after Shlee leaves, CJ, an older Inuit woman, comes to sit with us. She is a little shy, but wants to speak about her love for Mary. “She’s wonderful. Yes, truly wonderful. She’s one of the most amazing people I’ve ever met,” she says, before Mary throws her arms around her.
Après l’entrevue, elles sortent dans la: After the interview, they head out into the night with an all-women street patrol, which they call Girls Night. CJ is dressed warmly for the outing. “The vibe at Girls Night is good!” she exclaims. “It’s for young women like her that I save lives,” Mary exclaims, pointing at CJ. “If a man puts a hand on her, here’s what’s going to happen to him,” she threatens, raising her fist. “I love you,” CJ replies.
Mary Kelly reconnaît que son travail peu: Mary Kelly acknowledges that her work can also be heavy. She drinks alcohol to release the pressure, but she also turns to spiritual practices and relies on the support of her loved ones.
« J'ai suivi au moins six cures de désin: “I’ve been through at least six detox and treatment programs. I let go of some things while I was in treatment. I thought it was me, I was carrying things. It wasn’t me. I got those things out by sweating them out, like I’m doing now [in this interview]. I’m doing it with you,” she says, pointing at me and nodding.
« Laisser aller les choses ! J'ai appris: “Let things go! I learned how to do that. Because if you can’t get it out, I swear to you, you’ll carry it for days, the burden will be heavy, and you’ll die from it,” Mary explains, her gaze intense. “When I’m not drinking, I have to be like a ‘White Lady Mary,’” she says, exaggerating an upright posture and articulating her words excessively.
« Je suis fatiguée des convenances. Tout: “I’m tired of politeness and propriety. Everyone should be tired of it. Everyone should get to know the taste of snow. No one should feel uncomfortable sitting on the ground. No one,” she says.
Les gens dans la rue lui ont été d’un gr: The people on the street have been a great support to her, just as she is for them. “I’m in a housing program. I was homeless last year. I told myself that if I can fall and get back up, fall again and get back up again, a lot of other people can too. I’m not special. I’m strong, but I’m not special. Those people [out there] are special,” she says, pointing outside. “They’re the ones who say, ‘Mary, you’re going to make it, don’t worry about what’s going on. You can do it.’”
« Je n'ai jamais entendu cela dans ma pr: “I never heard that in my own family. Nobody thinks that when you sit down with these ‘poor bastards,’ as they call them…” She speaks aloud in Inuktitut, searching for the right word in English. “Hobo,” she says, laughing. “That’s a funny word. You wouldn’t imagine these people have a strength whose extent you can only grasp if you sit down with them,” she says.
Alors que des organismes communautaires: As community organizations and governments look for ways to “end homelessness,” Mary believes it’s important to work upstream. “A real leader doesn’t just move forward. A real leader is at the bottom of the ladder, pushing up. That’s what I’ve done. If a leader can’t sit here and share a bite with you, then we don’t need them,” Mary Kelly concludes.
